subject.title: Old Smile at the Roast
subject.author: Glyn Maxwell
subject.text:
Test for the Old Smile, they're going to roast it-
it'll have to keep its ends up all night,
for the secretary says she finds it creepy,
and the golfing partner says you got that right,

and the rival says it's fake, and the ambitious
junior makes his point with a few slides,
and the protege the Smile was always sweet to
walks up and says it turns his insides.

They harp on it, the bosses and the buddies,
and things get even better by these lights,
which is to say it's shredded like a secret,
which is to say it's one of the great nights;

and folks are saying so while they're still roasting:
they cry out to the Smile and it smiles back,
like something huge is burdening a hammock,
or is until you hear a frightful crack.-

And then you better run like you saw nothing.
And then you better run like you weren't there.
There is a line, it's long and isn't smiling.
You won't believe me when I tell you where.

title: Run Like You Weren't There
standfirst: Glyn Maxwell's poem spends three stanzas as an office comedy roast and one line deciding, without warning, that it has been describing a killing. Nothing in the sound of it changes to tell you so.

sections.heading: The Joke That Keeps a Straight Face
sections.body:
For three stanzas this reads like an office comedy. A colleague's reputation, nicknamed the Old Smile, gets the standard public flaying: the secretary who always found it creepy, the golfing partner backing her up, the rival calling it fake, the ambitious junior making his case with slides. That is the whole shape of a roast — an old face publicly mocked so everyone can then say how fond of it they really are.

Then, without changing gear, Maxwell has the room decide the mockery is going well because the target is now [shredded like a secret](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/51249/old-smile-at-the-roast), something huge is described as burdening a hammock, and the noise stops with [a frightful crack](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/51249/old-smile-at-the-roast). The last stanza drops the joke's vocabulary entirely and gives a flat instruction instead: [run like you saw nothing](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/51249/old-smile-at-the-roast), [run like you weren't there](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/51249/old-smile-at-the-roast). Nothing announces that the poem has stopped being funny. The same bouncing rhythm that carried the golfing partner's one-liner carries the order to flee whatever has just happened.

sections.heading: A Ballad Quatrain in a Suit
sections.body:
Every stanza here is a quatrain, and every one rhymes only its second and fourth lines — night/right, slides/insides, lights/nights, back/crack, there/where — while the first and third lines are left unrhymed, running on their own comma-spliced logic ("and the rival says it's fake, and the ambitious / junior makes his point with a few slides"). It is loose balladry: a chiming half-form loose enough to carry talky, over-the-shoulder sentences, but built to land a hard rhymed thud at the end of every unit regardless of what that unit has just said.

Reviewing Maxwell's 2008 collection Hide Now that same year, [Publishers Weekly](https://www.publishersweekly.com/9780547154107) wrote that he "stitches casual phrase work into bolts of meter and swaths of rhyme" — a fair description of what is happening in miniature here, a gossipy office voice locked into a form tight enough to make the ending's flatness land like a verdict rather than a punchline. The [same publisher's own cover copy](https://www.panmacmillan.com/authors/glyn-maxwell/hide-now/9780330456241) quotes a paper calling his facility with form "astonishing" — this poem is a compact demonstration of what that facility is actually for.

sections.heading: The Year of Robespierre and the Reverend
sections.body:
This poem was filed by Poetry to its July/August 2008 issue, the same year Maxwell published [Hide Now](https://www.panmacmillan.com/authors/glyn-maxwell/hide-now/9780330456241), a collection built around exactly this kind of scene. Its publisher describes a book in which "the past rears up again with its angry ghosts, the present is racked by its martial and climatic nightmares, and the future has already come and gone," reaching for Robespierre, Dick Cheney and the Reverend Jim Jones as its cast, with Cassandra — the seer nobody believed until it was too late — as its [presiding figure](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/5232338-hide-now).

Nothing confirms that this particular poem sits inside that book. But the machinery is the one Maxwell kept building that year: an ordinary social occasion — a tribunal, a sermon, a leaving party — that a crowd agrees to treat as harmless right up until it isn't, and then agrees just as readily to have never seen. Robespierre's own committees ran on denunciation between people who had known each other socially before they turned on each other publicly. "Old Smile at the Roast" borrows that shape and shrinks it to a single retirement do: colleagues who use the vocabulary of affection to conduct something closer to an execution, then close ranks around the silence afterward exactly as a tribunal's audience does.

sections.heading: Seven Years Inside Someone Else's Argument
sections.body:
Maxwell was born in 1962 in Welwyn Garden City, and started a postgraduate degree at Worcester College, Oxford, before leaving it in 1987 to study poetry and drama at Boston University under Derek Walcott. He stayed in America for most of the next two decades, teaching in Amherst and New York, and from 2001 to 2007 served as poetry editor of [The New Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyn_Maxwell) — meaning he spent the whole stretch from September 11 to the middle of the Iraq War inside a magazine that spent those years arguing, weekly, about what a frightened state was entitled to do to people it had decided were dangerous.

He had moved back to Britain by 2006, a New Generation poet since 1994 and an E. M. Forster Award winner since 1997, no longer literally sitting inside that argument. This poem reached print within roughly two years of the move — written, if not about that magazine's politics specifically, at least by someone who had just spent seven years watching a country decide, case by case, who got called a threat, and who got to walk away afterward and say they hadn't seen anything.

sections.heading: What Roasting Means Here
sections.body:
The title carries two meanings before the poem has done anything: a roast is a comic genre, the retirement lunch where everyone insults you affectionately, and also a method of destroying something with heat. Maxwell keeps both running at once. The Old Smile goes through a workplace ritual — a secretary's complaint, a slide deck from an ambitious junior — and also, apparently, an actual burning: it is watched, it smiles back at the crowd egging it on, and then something gives way with [a frightful crack](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/51249/old-smile-at-the-roast).

Calling the target Old Smile rather than a name does similar double work — a nickname a colleague might plausibly have, and also a description of the one feature left once everything else about a person has been stripped away, an expression stuck on a face that can no longer choose it. "Shredded like a secret" adds a third register: office-paper destruction, the kind a company does to make an inconvenient record disappear. None of these readings cancels the others out. The poem needs the office comedy to keep reading as an office comedy even while it describes something that ends with a crowd that scatters — that overlap is exactly how the crowd inside the poem gets away with not noticing.

sections.heading: The Line It Won't Name
sections.body:
Every earlier stanza describes this happening to other people — the secretary, the rival, the folks who are roasting. The last one turns and addresses "you" directly, and introduces an "I" that has stayed silent for nineteen lines: "You won't believe me when I tell you where." It is the poem's only first-person claim, and it spends the whole of it on a refusal. We get the slides, the hammock, the crack, but not the location of the line that is long and isn't smiling — the one image in the poem that isn't dressed up as an office joke.

That withholding reads as the point rather than a gap in the poem. A version that named the place would be reporting an incident; a poem that lays out the whole machinery of a public destruction and then declines, at the last possible moment, to say where the queue for it forms, is describing a habit instead — something that could be happening now, filed under a word as harmless as roast. Whatever Maxwell had in mind writing it, the poem ends exactly where the crowd inside it does: having watched enough to know something has gone badly wrong, and told, in its own last words, to behave as though they hadn't.
